speaker: Jordan
text: Our position is simple. Section four of the contract says changes must be in writing and signed by Pat.

speaker: Riley
text: Section four also says the owner's representative can approve field changes. Fawn is the representative.

speaker: Jordan
text: A field change is a wall moved six inches. This is four hundred thousand dollars of oak.

speaker: Morgan
text: The contract doesn't put a dollar limit on field changes. Read it.

speaker: Sam
text: It doesn't need to. Any court would read that clause narrowly.

speaker: Sandy
text: Any court would also look at six years of past practice. Fawn has approved upgrades on every job.

speaker: Pat
text: Past practice doesn't override an express written term.

speaker: Riley
text: It does when the other party has accepted the practice for years. That's course of dealing.

speaker: Jordan
text: Was there a signed change order for the oak? Yes or no.

speaker: Sandy
text: There was an email from Fawn approving it.

speaker: Jordan
text: An email is not a signed change order.

speaker: Morgan
text: In this industry an email from the owner's rep is exactly that.

speaker: Sam
text: Industry custom doesn't rewrite the contract either.

speaker: Riley
text: So your argument is that Fawn had no authority at all?

speaker: Pat
text: Her authority was limited. She acted outside it.

speaker: Sandy
text: She acted in your best interest, as always. The original oak spec would have failed inspection.

speaker: Jordan
text: Then the right move was to call Pat, not to approve it herself.

speaker: Morgan
text: Pat was unreachable for two weeks.

speaker: Pat
text: Unreachable is not the same as having delegated authority.

speaker: Riley
text: What does the contract say about emergencies?

speaker: Sam
text: Nothing specific. Which means the default rule applies: written approval.

speaker: Sandy
text: Which means a court decides, and that takes two years.

speaker: Jordan
text: If that's where this ends up, so be it.

speaker: Morgan
text: Let's go back to the clause. Section four, paragraph two, defines representative.

speaker: Pat
text: And paragraph three limits what the representative may approve.

speaker: Riley
text: Paragraph three says material substitutions of equal value. Oak for oak.

speaker: Sam
text: Oak for oak at three times the price is not equal value.

speaker: Sandy
text: Equal in function. The spec never set a price.

speaker: Jordan
text: We're going in circles. Our position stands.

speaker: Morgan
text: So does ours. We'll see you in court.
